answer:
The concept is clear and sympathetic, but the submission reads as an idea with enthusiasm rather than a validated venture. Priorities for improvement, roughly in order of impact:

1) Build the unit economics. This is the biggest gap. The core claim (a fee per jar lower than the cost of new jars) is untested, and the plan never quantifies the costs it names. Show a per-jar cost stack: prepaid outbound mailer, return postage (glass is heavy and fragile, so round-trip shipping plus outbound shipping of cleaned jars back to the maker could easily exceed the $1-3 cost of a new jar), wax removal, washing, sanitizing, inspection, breakage and rejection rates, labor, and dashboard costs. Then compare against what makers actually pay for new jars and propose a price point with a margin. If the numbers do not work, say so and explain what would have to be true (volume, regional hubs, bulk consolidation) to make them work.

2) Replace assertions with evidence. 'Early feedback has been positive' and 'people said the idea was interesting' are weak signals. Report concrete data: how many makers and customers participated, how many jars were mailed versus how many were distributed (return rate), time and cost per jar in the prototype, breakage rate, and whether any maker would pay or commit to a paid pilot. Letters of intent or even a handful of signed pilot agreements would be far stronger than friends and family reactions.

3) Address the demand risk head-on. The plan itself identifies customer inaction as the biggest competitor, yet offers no mechanism to overcome it. Describe how you will drive return rates (incentives such as discounts or credits on the next candle, reminders, convenience features) and cite benchmarks from comparable reuse programs. Since makers pay per returned jar, return rate directly determines your revenue, so this belongs in the model.

4) Do real market sizing. 'Thousands of makers' and 'a very large number of jars' is not sizing. Use a bottom-up approach: number of target small makers, average jars sold per year, realistic adoption share, return rate, and resulting jars and revenue in years 1-3. Also address the geographic problem: makers and customers are spread nationally while you operate from one workspace, so explain how you handle cross-country shipping or whether you start regionally.

5) Sharpen the competitive analysis. Name specific competitors (general reuse platforms, brands with refill programs, candle makers who already run their own take-back) and compare on price, convenience, and target customer. Be careful with the claim that large brands will not serve small makers; explain why general reuse services could not simply add candle support. Articulate what is defensible beyond focus: relationships, data, logistics density, or switching costs.

6) Address operational and regulatory realities. Cover scalability of cleaning beyond a shared kitchen (equipment, space, throughput), food-grade versus non-food sanitation standards, wax disposal, product safety and liability when a maker refills a reused jar, and jar standardization (makers use many different jar shapes, which complicates sorting and matching returns to the right maker). Note also the open question of whether jars return to the original maker or a pooled system.

7) Strengthen the business model section. Pick a primary revenue model with draft prices, state who pays for postage, and test willingness to pay with a few makers. The premium dashboard is speculative; either drop it or support it with evidence that makers want it. Quantify the environmental claims (glass avoided, carbon saved) with cited methodology, since the dashboard's credibility depends on it, and consider that shipping emissions may offset some of the benefit.

8) Provide a basic financial model and a specific funding plan. Even a simple 12-24 month projection with explicit assumptions, break-even volume, and monthly burn would help. State the amount requested and break the use of funds into line items with costs. Define pilot success metrics (for example, number of makers, jars processed, return rate, cost per jar) so judges can see what the money will prove.

9) Address team gaps. All three founders are students with no consumer products, logistics, or candle industry experience. Name specific advisors you are pursuing or have approached, and show relevant commitment such as time per week and plans beyond graduation.

10) Tighten the writing. The document is clean but generic and hedged ('we believe', 'we hope', 'we think'). Lead with quantified claims, add a short traction and metrics section, and include visuals such as a process flow diagram, a mockup of the dashboard, and a cost-per-jar table. Replace repeated admissions of what has not been done with a clear timeline showing what will be done, by when, and what each step will validate.

Bottom line: the team should convert the narrative into a testable hypothesis, with measured pilot data, a per-jar cost model, a return-rate strategy, and evidence that at least a few makers will pay.
